chapter_theme: A catalogue of false friendship: the self-serving, the unreliable, fools, jesters and the two-faced. Its rhetoric of comparison ranks all of them below loneliness and even below enemies.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: harm of such friendship in general (811), then by type: those who look to their own gain (812-813), those who fail in need (814-815), fools, jesters and those who won't do what they can (816-818), and deceivers (819-820).

811.reading: Though they seem to drink you up, the friendship of those without character is better shrinking than growing.
811.nuance: பருகுவார் is the language of passion. Parimelazhagar cites a matching line of poetry and Manakkudavar adds 'with the eyes'. The verse warns that intensity is not evidence. The advice is modest too, since it only says that shrinking is better.

812.reading: What does it matter whether one gains or loses the friendship of misfits who are friends when there is profit and leave when there is none?
812.nuance: The rhetorical shrug is the point. Parimelazhagar concludes that one should simply be neutral toward them (நொதுமல்). They are neither to be sought nor fought, which sets them apart from the verses that say to run.

813.reading: Friends who weigh what they stand to gain, those who take what they get, and thieves are all alike.
813.nuance: The middle term in the verse says only 'those who take what they get'. It is the commentators who identify them as prostitutes. In the verse's shape, the calculation of friends is the real target and the other two are comparisons.

814.reading: Better solitude than having as one's own those like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle.
814.nuance: The horse has been carrying its rider well until the moment that counts. Parimelazhagar also notes the verse doesn't praise solitude, which is only less bad. Valluvar isn't recommending it.

815.reading: It is better not to get than to get the poor friendship of the small, who are no protection even after one has made them friends.
815.nuance: ஏமம் brings in the guard of 781 again: a friend who doesn't protect has failed the definition.

positions.position: The small are base people in general, whose failure is that they leave in ruin.
The small are particular kinds of people, gamblers, hunters and women among them, a gendered list which the verse doesn't contain.
positions.quote: சிறியார் - சூதர், வேட்டைக் காரர், பெண்டிர் போல்வார்.

816.reading: Being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool.
816.nuance: ஏதின்மை is literally not-belonging. Pope and the commentators read it as enmity. Parimelazhagar's argument is that the enmity of the wise does no harm while the fool's friendship does every harm.

817.reading: Ten crore times better than friendship of the kind that is all laughter is what comes from enemies.
817.nuance: The multiplier goes up ten times from 816. Parimelazhagar says even the pains that enemies cause exceed the pleasures of these friends, identifies them as hangers-on who amuse for profit, and dismisses other commentators' readings as ungrammatical.

818.reading: With those who make hard work of what they could easily do, let the friendship slip without a word.
818.nuance: A practical subtlety. Parimelazhagar says speaking would only lead them to patch things up and go on, so the silence is tactical. It is the opposite of a formal break.

819.reading: Even in a dream, the bond with those whose deeds are one thing and words another is bitter.
819.nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss is exact: enemies in deed and friends in word. The dream adds that the harm follows into sleep, a place where in other verses love is what lives.

820.reading: Take care not to come near at all to the bond of those who are friendly at home and defame you in the assembly.
820.nuance: The contrast is between private and public, and it's the public that matters: a friend is tested by what is said in the மன்று. எனைத்தும் leaves no room for degree, unlike the 'better to shrink' of 811.

links.note: 784 says friendship exists to rebuke, openly and in advance. 818 says that with a certain kind of friend, say nothing and let it fade. Whether one rebukes turns out to depend on whether the friend is still worth the rebuke.
784 says friendship isn't for laughter. 817 raises that to a ten-crore disadvantage against enemies. A verse about purpose becomes a verdict on a whole class of companion.

911 says the women who desire wealth rather than the man bring ruin through sweet words. 813 applies the same logic to friends who calculate, and the comparison runs the other way: chapter 92's accusation is made first of men's friendships.

source_issues: 812: The Tamil of the verse reads அறின்ஙருஉம் in kg/core/kural.jsonl. Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அறின் ஒரூஉம், so this looks like a corrupted character.
816: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.
